queries.problem_constrained: For a high-entropy alloy designed as a single-phase solid solution and strengthened by local chemical order, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why toughness is lost after thermal exposure in a tempering-relevant regime under subsequent mechanical loading? Define a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial unexposed state, identify applicable exposure and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.
queries.expert_context: Temper embrittlement in conventional alloys has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation or brittle grain-boundary precipitation, whereas high-entropy alloys exhibit thermodynamic and kinetic complexity that can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation. Earlier work tailored local chemical order to improve strength–ductility synergy, but did not establish how such order evolves during thermal exposure or whether that evolution degrades toughness; equilibration may also challenge the intended single-phase state. Under the constraint of a compositionally complex, initially single-phase high-entropy alloy strengthened by local chemical order, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why tempering-like embrittlement occurs? Specify a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the unexposed baseline, the exposure and loading boundaries over which it should apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.
